AC9M10SP03.title: Spatial Algorithms and Digital Design
AC9M10SP03.meaning: Design, test and refine algorithms or digital procedures for spatial problems, then justify the solution.
AC9M10SP03.prereq: Revise Cartesian coordinates, transformations, angle and length relationships, scale, basic geometric reasoning and the idea of an algorithm as an unambiguous sequence of steps.
AC9M10SP03.reason: Design an algorithm for placing four equally spaced points around a circle and connecting them to form a square. Test your method for different circle radii and centres, explain which properties remain invariant, and justify why the output is a square.
AC9M10SP03.teacher: Assess process evidence: algorithm version 1, test cases, identified failure, refinement and final justification. This is richer than grading only the final diagram.
AC9M10SP03.parent: Ask your child to explain the instructions so clearly that another person could reproduce the design without seeing the original. Ambiguity is the key thing to remove.
AC9M10SP03.vic: VC2M10ASP06 — Level 10A Space; Level 10 Space provides supporting knowledge
AC9M10SP03.nsw: Stage 5 Paths Geometrical figures and proof / Introduction to networks; Working mathematically

AC9M10ST01.title: Statistical Claims, Bias and Media Reports
AC9M10ST01.meaning: Evaluate statistical claims in media by examining evidence, sampling, representation, bias, inference and ethical issues.
AC9M10ST01.prereq: Revise percentages, averages, data displays, sampling ideas and basic interpretation of graphs and tables.
AC9M10ST01.reason: Find or invent a plausible media claim such as 'students using App X improve marks by 40%'. Write a statistical audit covering sample selection, comparison group, measurement, absolute versus relative change, causation, missing information and ethical considerations.
AC9M10ST01.teacher: Use real headlines but grade the reasoning structure, not students' opinions about the topic. Require evidence-specific language such as 'selection bias because…'.
AC9M10ST01.parent: When you see a statistic in the news, ask together: 'Compared with what?', 'Out of how many?', and 'Who was included?'. Those three questions expose many weak claims.
AC9M10ST01.nsw: Stage 5 Core Data classification, visualisation and analysis; Path Data analysis and statistical enquiry

AC9M10ST02.title: Boxplots and Continuous Data Distributions
AC9M10ST02.meaning: Compare continuous numerical distributions using boxplots and other displays, discussing centre, spread, shape and outliers.
AC9M10ST02.prereq: Revise ordering numerical data, median, range, percentages, histograms and dot plots.
AC9M10ST02.reason: Two schools have the same median exam score of 70. School A has Q1=66,Q3=75; School B has Q1=55,Q3=84 and several high outliers. Write a careful comparison of typical performance, consistency and what the outliers do and do not imply.
AC9M10ST02.teacher: Pair boxplots with dot plots or histograms of the same data so students see what summarisation hides. Mark comparison sentences for evidence + context.
AC9M10ST02.parent: Ask your child what the box, median line and whiskers each mean. Then ask which group is more consistent, not just which has the higher median.
hints: treat outliers as flags, not automatic deletions
AC9M10ST02.nsw: Stage 5 Core Data classification, visualisation and analysis; Path Data analysis and statistical enquiry

AC9M10ST03.title: Scatterplots and Bivariate Association
AC9M10ST03.meaning: Construct and interpret scatterplots, describing association by direction, strength and linearity without confusing correlation with causation.
AC9M10ST03.prereq: Revise Cartesian coordinates, numerical variables, graph axes, data collection and interpreting trends.
AC9M10ST03.reason: A scatterplot of screen time and sleep duration shows a moderate negative association. Write three different plausible explanations for the pattern, including one involving a third variable, and explain why the scatterplot alone cannot choose among them.
AC9M10ST03.teacher: Give students several scatterplots with the same direction but different strength and form. Require full-sentence contextual descriptions rather than labels only.
AC9M10ST03.parent: Ask your child to describe a scatterplot without using the word 'causes'. Then ask what other explanation could produce the pattern.
AC9M10ST03.nsw: Stage 5 Core Data classification, visualisation and analysis; Path Data analysis and statistical enquiry

AC9M10ST04.title: Two-Way Tables and Categorical Relationships
AC9M10ST04.meaning: Construct two-way tables and use counts and proportions to investigate possible relationships between categorical variables.
AC9M10ST04.prereq: Revise percentages, fractions, categorical variables and reading frequency tables.
AC9M10ST04.reason: Create a two-way table for 160 students classified by year level and whether they participate in school sport. Use unequal group sizes, calculate within-year percentages, then write a conclusion that distinguishes association from causation.
AC9M10ST04.teacher: Ask two opposite questions from the same table—'of Year 10s, who…?' and 'of those who…, how many are Year 10?'—to make denominator choice explicit.
AC9M10ST04.parent: Use a simple household or sports table and ask your child which total should go underneath the fraction. Denominator choice is the conceptual heart of this topic.
hints: identify the question before choosing denominator
AC9M10ST04.nsw: Stage 5 Core Data classification, visualisation and analysis; Path Data analysis and statistical enquiry

AC9M10ST05.title: Bivariate Statistical Investigations
AC9M10ST05.meaning: Plan, conduct and report bivariate statistical investigations while recognising limitations on the inferences that can be made.
AC9M10ST05.prereq: Revise sampling, numerical/categorical variables, two-way tables, scatterplots, centre/spread and the difference between association and causation.
AC9M10ST05.reason: Plan a complete investigation into whether commute time is associated with lateness among Year 10 students. Specify variables, units, sampling, collection procedure, representation, likely confounders, ethical/privacy issues and the wording of a cautious conclusion.
AC9M10ST05.teacher: Have students submit a one-page investigation plan for approval before collecting data. This prevents weak questions and teaches that design quality determines the value of later calculations.
AC9M10ST05.parent: Ask your child who their conclusion is really about—the people they sampled or a wider population—and what could make the two groups different.
AC9M10ST05.nsw: Stage 5 Path Data analysis and statistical enquiry, supported by Core data analysis

AC9M10P01.title: Conditional Probability Language
AC9M10P01.meaning: Use conditional-probability language precisely and identify how the relevant sample space changes when information is given.
AC9M10P01.prereq: Revise fractions, probability, two-way tables, Venn-style set thinking and basic event notation.
AC9M10P01.reason: A school reports: '80% of students who achieved an A used the revision platform.' A parent interprets this as '80% of platform users get an A.' Explain the conditional-probability error and construct a numerical example where the first statement is true but the parent's statement is far from true.
AC9M10P01.teacher: Read conditional statements aloud and have students physically cover rows/columns outside the conditioned group before calculating. This makes the denominator change visible.
AC9M10P01.parent: Ask 'Who are we talking about now?' whenever a question says 'given' or 'of'. If your child names the restricted group before calculating, they are likely on track.
hints: rebuild the denominator from the conditioned group
AC9M10P01.nsw: Stage 5 Core Probability; Path Further probability

AC9M10P02.title: Conditional Probability Simulations
AC9M10P02.meaning: Design repeated chance experiments and digital simulations for conditional probability, then interpret long-run results and model limitations.
AC9M10P02.prereq: Revise relative frequency, multi-step probability, sampling with and without replacement, conditional-probability language and simple digital random-number tools.
AC9M10P02.reason: Design a simulation for a bag with 4 red, 3 blue and 2 green counters, drawing two without replacement. Estimate P(second is red | first is blue). Specify the digital representation, update rule, trial filtering and how you would judge whether the estimate is stable.
AC9M10P02.teacher: Have students predict before simulation, then compare small and large runs. Include one deliberately flawed model and ask students to diagnose why more trials do not repair it.
AC9M10P02.parent: Use simple cards or coloured objects first. Ask what changes after an item is removed and not replaced, then connect that idea to the digital simulation.
hints: filter by the condition before dividing
update probabilities when no replacement occurs
more trials reduce random noise, not model bias
AC9M10P02.nsw: Stage 5 Core Probability; Path Further probability
